faqs.q: How do I convert my hourly rate to an annual salary?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work per week, then by 52. For a standard full-time week of 38 hours, the formula is hourly × 38 × 52. This gives your gross annual pay before tax and other deductions.

faqs.q: Does the calculator include casual loading?
faqs.a: Yes, the timesheet has a checkbox to add 25% casual loading on top of your base hourly rate. Do not type a rate that already includes casual loading; use the base rate and tick the box.

Super guarantee is 12% of your ordinary earnings, paid on top of your gross pay by your employer. It is not deducted from your take-home pay. The calculator estimates super up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year.

bodyMarkdown:
## How to Use a Take Home Pay Calculator for Your Hourly Rate

If you’re paid by the hour or considering a salary offer, a **take home pay calculator** helps you see the full picture: annual gross pay, fortnightly amounts, tax, Medicare, and super. This article explains the maths behind the conversion, the assumptions we make, and how to interpret the results.

### The Basic Formula: Hourly × Hours per Week × 52

Annual gross pay = hourly rate × hours per week × 52 weeks. This assumes you work the same number of hours every week, with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, allowances, or salary sacrifice. For a standard full-time role, we assume **38 hours per week** – the typical ordinary hours under many awards and the National Employment Standards.

For example, the **National Minimum Wage** from 1 July 2026 is $26.44 per hour. For 38 hours, the weekly pay is $1,004.90 (as set by the Fair Work Commission). Multiply by 52 weeks: annual gross pay is approximately $52,255. If you work a different number of hours, adjust the formula accordingly. The [the timesheet](/) lets you enter any base rate and hours.

### Fortnightly Pay: A Handy Midpoint

Many employers pay fortnightly. Simply multiply your weekly gross by two. Using the minimum wage example: $1,004.90 × 2 = $2,009.80 per fortnight before tax. A take home pay calculator can show you the after-tax amount for each pay period.

### Tax and Medicare: What Comes Off

Your take-home pay is your gross pay minus tax and the Medicare levy. For the 2026–27 income year, the Australian Tax Office’s resident tax rates are:

- Nil on the first $18,200
- 15% on the next $26,800 (up to $45,000)
- 30% on the next $90,000 (up to $135,000)
- 37% on the next $55,000 (up to $190,000)
- 45% on amounts above $190,000

Medicare levy is generally 2% of your taxable income. The calculator uses the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds because the 2026–27 thresholds were not confirmed at the time of preparation. This means the estimate is close but not exact if you qualify for a reduction.

Let’s work through the minimum wage example ($52,255 annual):
- Tax: $0 on first $18,200; $4,020 on the next $26,800 (15%); $2,176.50 on the remaining $7,255 (30%) = total tax $6,196.50
- Medicare: $1,045.10 (2% of $52,255)
- Total deductions: $7,241.60
- Estimated take-home: $45,013.40 per year, or about $865.64 per week.

Remember: this is an estimate. It does not include HELP repayments, the Medicare levy surcharge, or salary packaging. For a personalised result, use the [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) section of our site.

### Superannuation: Paid on Top

Super guarantee is 12% of your ordinary earnings, paid by your employer on top of your gross pay. It is not deducted from your pay. For the minimum wage example, the super contribution would be $52,255 × 12% = $6,270.60 per year, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830. The calculator shows an estimate of super, but your actual amount depends on your award or agreement. See [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) for more details.

### Casual Loading and Award Rates

If you’re a casual employee, you’re entitled to a 25% loading on top of the base rate. The National Minimum Wage for casuals is $33.05 per hour ($26.44 + 25%). **Do not type a rate that already includes casual loading** into the timesheet. Instead, enter the base rate and tick the “casual loading” checkbox – the calculator adds the 25% automatically. This is explained on the [casual loading](/topics/casual-loading) page.

Award rates can be higher than the minimum. The Fair Work Ombudsman publishes pay guides for each industry. Our [pay guides](/blog) page links to the official sources. If you’re covered by an award, use the correct base rate for your classification.

### Average Weekly Earnings: A Benchmark

The Australian Bureau of Statistics reports **Average Weekly Earnings** for May 2026. Full-time adult ordinary time earnings averaged $2,083.70 per week. All employees (including part-time) averaged $1,579.20 per week. These are averages, not medians for a specific job. Use them as a general benchmark. For more context, see [average pay](/topics/average-pay).

### What the Calculator Does Not Include

Our take home pay calculator is a tool for quick estimates. It assumes:
- The same hourly rate every week
- No unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances
- No salary sacrifice or packaging
- Super at 12% of ordinary earnings only, capped at the maximum contribution base
- Tax using the 2026–27 resident scale with full tax-free threshold
- Medicare using 2025–26 single reduction thresholds

It does not deduct HELP, the Medicare levy surcharge, or any other adjustments. Always check with a tax professional or the Australian Taxation Office for your exact situation.

### Putting It All Together

Whether you’re negotiating a salary, comparing job offers, or budgeting, a take home pay calculator gives you a clear starting point. Start with your hourly rate, multiply by your weekly hours and 52 weeks, then subtract estimated tax and Medicare. Add super on top to see your total employment cost. Use [the timesheet](/) to run the numbers for any rate, and explore our [reference tables](/data) for tax brackets and super caps.

Remember: the National Minimum Wage is $26.44 per hour from 1 July 2026. If you earn less than that, your employer may be breaking the law. Check the [minimum wage](/topics/minimum-wage) page for current rates and your entitlements.
